newsitem.title: UK: BA strike enters second day, chaos for passengers.
newsitem.headline: BA strike enters second day, chaos for passengers.

text.p: Air travellers braced for more disruptions on Thursday as British Airways' cabin crew began the second day of a strike with no solution in sight.

As both sides squabbled over the legality of the 72-hour work stoppage, more than 25,000 passengers were left stranded on Wednesday when the airline cancelled half of its flights out of London and up to 30 percent of the 1,000 flights it operates worldwide each day.

BA's Director of Human Resources Mervyn Walker said the airline hoped to operate 20 percent more flights on Thursday, but a spokesman for the Transport and General Workers Union (T&G) doubted it would make much difference.
"Twenty percent of very little is not much," Andrew Murray told Reuters.
BA claims the strike over allowances and overtime and its plans to cut 42 million pounds ($71 million) from its operating budget is illegal because of discrepancies in the strike ballot.
It threatened to sue the main cabin crew union for losses.
But the union was equally adamant about its position. "We have absolute confidence in the legality of our conduct," said Murray, adding that the union was ready to negotiate at any time.
The union said it was prepared to help the airline find the money, but it was not prepared to have new terms and conditions imposed on its members.
The apparent deadlock between the two side was more bad news for travellers.
"I can't wait to get home and I'm never coming here again, and never flying British Airways again," said a woman stranded at London's Heathrow airport.
The airline's normally bustling terminal at the airport was unusually quiet after the strike began at 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Wednesday. It is due to last until early on Saturday.
Striking workers on picket lines defiantly waved banners as travellers arrived at the airport. Pickets were also stationed outside other British airports.

British Airways said it estimated that about 1,000 cabin staff had reported for work by the end of Wednesday, but more than 1,500 had called in sick, rather than admit they were striking, for fear of reprisals from the airline.
Another 160 defied the airline and said they were on strike.

Management had warned that employees could lose travel perks and opportunities for promotion if they went on strike. But the airline denied union claims that employees had been bullied and threatened with reprisals.
"What we have done is to point out the potential legal consequences of being on strike. Our emphasis is on urging people to work. We have not threatened them," an airline spokesman said.
The airline said it needed between 1,800-2,000 staff to run a full programme on a normal day.

BA faced more problems with a separate dispute with ground crew over the sale of its catering division at Heathrow. The workers were expected to be balloted late on Wednesday about whether they would accept BA's offer to resolve the row.
The result of their vote is due to be announced late on Thursday.

The Daily Mail newspaper said in a front-page report that BA was bringing in "strikebusters" to fill staffing gaps caused by the strike. "British Airways revealed that 500 new recruits were being trained to take over from striking airline cabin staff and a further 3,000 were waiting in the wings," said the newspaper.
No independent confirmation of the report was available early on Thursday.
